AI Lab

Introduction
QUINTON GILLANDERS
SOFTWARE DEVELOPER THAT LIKES BUILDING COOL APPS

By the end of this
lesson, you will:
UNDERSTAND WHAT AI IS (HISTORY, DEFINITION, COMMON USE)
RECOGNIZE AI IN EVERYDAY LIFE (SOCIAL MEDIA, GOOGLE MAPS, NETFLIX, SIRI, CHATGPT, ETC).
BUILD CURIOSITY AND CONFIDENCE IN ENGAGING WITH AI.

Have you
used AI
Before?

Lesson 1 - What is AI?
AI learns from lots of information
AI can answer questions and solve problems
AI can create stories, pictures and music
While it is helpful, it can also make some mistakes

Human Intelligence VS Artificial
Intelligence
Humans AI
Have Emotions No Emotions
Creative Learns from examples
Can use common sense Follows patterns
Learn from life experiences Learns from data

How does AI Actually Work?
AI Looks at millions of examples
It finds patterns, and uses those patterns to make predictions
Example:
It will look at thousands of cat photos, learn that they have pointy ears, and then
will be able to recognize another cat.

How does AI Actually Work?
When given a task, AI will use the patterns to predict outputs. Some
more examples:
- Typing "hav" - autocorrect will predict "have"
- Spotify will recommend songs like the ones you already love
- TikTok and Youtube will show videos based on what you watch and
rewatch

Icebreaker: AI in my pocket
Step 1: List 3 ways you already use AI in your daily life.
(Hint: think about social media, apps, games or
devices at home!)
Step 2: Share and compare!
Turn to a partner and share one of your examples.
- Did they come up with the same ones as you?
- Or did they think of something you hadn't noticed?
Also be ready to share one cool example with the
class!

Activity 1: Design your own AI!
Invent a brand-new AI tool that could be useful (or
fun!) in everyday life. Give it a name, explain what
data it would need to be trained on, and describe
what it could do.
1) 2) 4) What is the name of the AI?
What data does it learn from?
3) How does it work?
What problem does it solve? And why it's fun!
5) Bonus Challenge: Draw a quick sketch of what
your AI could look like!

Different Types of AI in daily life!
AI isn't just one thing, it's everywhere. From the moment you wake up
and check your phone, to the time you go to bed scrolling through
your favorite apps.
Examples:
Netflix recommending a new show
Snapchat applying a funny filter to your face
Your phone suggesting the quickest route to your school

Different Types of AI in daily life!
Common types you see every day:
• Recommendation AI
• Recognition AI
• Language AI
• Predictive AI
• Creative AI

Lesson 2 - Writing Prompts

By the end of this lesson -
You will be able to:
Understand what a prompt is and how it guides AI responses.
Use effective structures when writing prompts (role, task,
context, format).
Write clear, creative and practical prompts that produce
strong results.

What is a
prompt?
A prompt is an instruction
or question you give to an
AI tool.
It is how we communicate
with AI and tell it what we
want it to do, how we
want it done, and what
kind of response we can
expect
The AI's output is only as
good as your input!

What is a
prompt?
Imagine if you're asking a
friend to draw a picture of
you
If you just said, "Draw
something", that would
mean anything.
Now imagine you ask:
"Draw a cute cartoon cat
wearing sunglasses and
holding an ice cream"
Result

Activity 1 – Prompt
Detectives!
The goal for this activity: Spot the most effective
prompt.
Below are three prompts AI prompts
"Write about animals"
"Write a fun paragraph about why penguins can't fly"
"Animals info please"
Which is best and why?
How could you improve the other two prompts?

Activity 2 – Draw it
with words
Your goal is to visualize how clarity shapes
creativity.
Imagine you're asking AI to "draw"
something using words.
Write one short vague prompt and one
clear descriptive prompt for the same
image.
Examples:
Vague: "Draw something cool"
Specific: "Draw a robot surfing a rainbow
wave under a starry sky."

Activity 2 – Draw it
with words
Reflection:
What details made the second prompt
stronger?
The Prompt Formula

Every strong prompt usually includes four key parts that
work together to tell the AI exactly what to do and how
to do it
Part What it means Example
Role Tell the Ai who it
should be or act as
"You are a travel
agent..."
Task Tell it what to do – the
main goal or activity
"...write a short
itinerary..."
Context Give background
details or information
to help the AI tailor it's
response
"… for a family visiting
Japan..."
Format Explain how you want
the answer to look –
list, paragraph, table,
script, etc.
"… as a bullet-point
list."

Why each part
matters
When you give AI a role, you're telling it who to
become for your request
If you say "You're a teacher" - The AI explains
things simply
If you say "You're a scientist" - The AI becomes
more technical and detailed.
Some more examples:
"You are a film critic, write a review for Toy Story 5"
"You are a primary school teacher, explain
photosynthesis to Year 5 students"
"You are a travel blogger, describe how your trip
to Paris was".

Role Roulette
GROUP GAME

Role Roulette
Part 1
Instructions
Your goal is to experiment with how changing the role
impacts the AI's tone and response.
I will write the different roles clearly on the whiteboard
- Artist
- Teacher
- CEO
- Wizard
- Astronaut
Example:
"Describe how to make a sandwich"
Artist: "You are an artist describing a sandwich as a
masterpiece".
Scientist: "You are a scientist explaining the sandwich
process step-by-step".

Role Roulette Part
2 Instructions
Some prompts don't quite hit the mark,
can you fix them?
Here are some weak prompts:
1. "Write about space."
2. "You are a chef. Talk about
food"
3. "Make a poem about love"
Your job is to rewrite each one to
make it strong by adding all four
parts – Role, Task. Context and
Format
Example fix:
"You are a science teacher.
Explain how recycling helps the
planet to a Year 6 class using
simple bullet points".

End of
Lesson 2!

Lesson 3 - Advanced
Prompting and
Refinement

By the end of this lesson,
you will be able to:
Learn advanced strategies, role assignment,
multi-step prompts, iteration
Compare simple vs advanced prompting
Develop problem solving skills with AI

Simple Vs Advanced
Prompting
Simple Prompt - "Write a story about
friendship"
Advanced Prompt: "You are a friendly Year
7 teacher, write a warm story about
friendship using 100 words".

Technique 1 – Role
Assignment
Tell AI who to be:
"You are a history teacher..."
"You are a fun inventor..."
"You are a kind coach..."
Good roles, better tone ideas!

Technique 2 – Multi
Step Prompts
Break big tasks into steps:
- Plan
- Create
- Review
Example:
"First, list 3 ideas for a school recycling
campaign. Then choose the best one.
Finally, write a poster slogan."

Technique 3 –
Iteration (Improve it!)
You don't have to stop at the first answer!
Improve it by giving feedback to the AI
Examples:
"Make it shorter and funnier"
"Add examples for Year 7 students"

Activity – Prompt
makeover challenge
AI won't always get it right the first time, and that's okay!
In this activity, you will practice iteration, which means
improving your prompts through feedback and testing
Start with this simple prompt: "Write about friendship"
Improve it 3 times (make it clearer each round)
Share your best version!

End of
Lesson 3!

Lesson 4 - Responsible
and Ethical AI Use

By the end of this will be able to:
Use AI effectively and safely
Understand common problems (bias, plagiarism, misinformation, privacy)
Understand how to be a responsible AI user
lesson, you

The 4 biggest things
to watch out for
Bias – AI can copy unfair ideas
from its training data
Plagiarism – Don't copy AI work as
your own
Misinformation – AI can make
mistakes or invent facts
Privacy – Don't share personal
information

Final Activity – Would
you risk it?
This is a mini ethical decision game. There is no right or
wrong – just your judgment.
Instructions:
Read each scenario on the next slide
Choose if it is okay to use AI or not okay to use AI
Write a one sentence explanation of why
Discuss your reasoning with a partner or a small group

Final Activity – Would
you risk it?
Scenarios
Your group decides to use AI to generate half of a report
to save time, but only one member plans to declare it in
the submission notes.
After receiving teacher feedback, you paste your whole
essay into ai and ask it to "rewrite based on this
feedback" instead of revising sections yourself.
You use AI to help check grammar and structure before
submission.
Before an exam, you use AI to practice by asking it to
quiz you with sample questions based on your notes. You
double-check the answers yourself afterward.
You use AI to summarise lecture notes you already wrote
yourself
